Receiving a request, entering it into another system and deciding what happens next are separate assignments. A residential service business should price the assignment it actually wants, rather than treating every listed service as part of an entry offer.

Published by Revo, a competing AI receptionist provider. This guide uses public documentation reviewed October 30, 2026; it does not report hands-on testing, measured performance or customer results.

The supplier reviewed here is [CBSI Holdings](https://cbsiholdings.com/answering-services/), whose answering page describes American live operators, basic message handling and call patching alongside broader custom services. Its published starting amount is $35 per month for 30 minutes of on-phone time. That wording does not establish that all advertised administrative work is included.

Keep that specific company and page attached to your proposal. A similar corporate name is not evidence of the same reception product. Ask the quoted agreement to identify the supplier and the service being purchased.

## Separate conversation time from work surrounding the call

For a small repair office, the original request might be straightforward: collect a homeowner's return number, address and description of the problem. The office may then need someone to create a record, check an existing request or find the employee authorized to respond. Those activities can require additional access and different responsibilities.

Do not estimate the bill from conversation length alone until the supplier explains the billing rules. Ask whether time spent preparing a record, attempting a patch, waiting for an employee or completing an authorized system entry is counted, separately charged or outside scope. Leave the answers blank until the written offer resolves them.

| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Receive an ordinary repair request | An anonymized example and actual conversation duration | Required intake fields, billable time and delivery destination | Decide whether the requested work is offered |
| Patch a caller to the office | Available recipient and unavailable-recipient example | Whether attempted transfers or waiting count toward usage | Maintain an accurate recipient list |
| Add information to another system | A fictional record and the exact fields permitted | Whether entry is purchased, access requirements and its billing treatment | Authorize access and correct business decisions |
| Handle a question about an existing request | The information an authorized worker could consult | Whether the service may read, update or only collect a question | Own the answer when the record is missing or disputed |

Use a fictional homeowner who initially requests a repair and then says the address or requested work has changed. Would it send another message, revise an existing record or leave a clearly identified question for your office?

Inspect the expected output rather than accepting “customized service” as the complete answer.
